summarize, not surface: the approach seam
text:
*Refined by the user 2026-09-04, and the refinement changes the approach rather than adding to it:*
"when presenting an unassigned span for review, look back in the transcripts and summarize what was
happening."

**The word is /summarize/, and the paragraph above says the opposite** — "extracting it is mechanical
rather than a judgement call", with candidate evidence listed as files touched and prompt text. Those
are *signals*, and the ask is for *prose*. A reviewer looking at a span does not want four file paths
and a prompt fragment; they want a sentence that names the work. So this heading now spans a seam it
previously sat on one side of, and which side it lands on is the open question:

- *Mechanical*, as originally scoped: surface the evidence, let the human summarize. Cheap,
  deterministic, no new transport, and it degrades to the =5ff5a4b8= behaviour that already helped
  without closing the gap.
- *Judged*, which is what "summarize" literally asks for: a subagent reads the transcript window and
  writes the sentence. That is =295cde3a='s mechanism — the join is exact and measured, 28 of 28
  =resume= events matching a transcript timestamp within two seconds — and =0c8644ff= already settled
  the transport (=claude -p= asynchronously, since there is often no live session at review time).

*A worked instance, produced by hand the same day.* The span
=[2026-09-03 Thu 14:10]--[14:34]= came up in conversation and was reconstructed from the queue file
plus the session transcript: four turns, 0:05 of actual running inside 0:24 of wall clock, spent
relaying a code review, diagnosing why local =main= was 165 commits stale, checking that the posted
comments fell inside the right diff, and confirming =main= was still behind. That reconstruction took
one =jq= over the queue and a read of the turns, and it made the assignment obvious immediately —
"Review and planning", continuous with the interval already filed there at 14:34. **That is precisely
this heading's output, done manually**, which is the strongest evidence yet that it is worth
building; note it needed both corpora, not just the transcript.

*One caution the instance also produced.* Part of the supporting evidence had already been destroyed
by the time it was wanted: =.git/FETCH_HEAD= carried a timestamp inside the span, and a later =git
fetch= in the same session overwrote it. Filesystem mtimes are not a corpus. Whatever this builds
must read the queue and the transcripts, which are append-only, and not the working tree, which is
not.

active marking reverses a measured decision
text:
*Checked 2026-09-04, prompted by the user asking what a no-run span actually writes — and the answer
changes what "mark it active" costs.*

**A span with no runs is not a no-op.** =--review-apply-clock= writes no CLOCK line for it, and does
write a =:LOGBOOK:= annotation, gated on =(unless observed)=. Its docstring gives the reason: "the
guideposts are real evidence that something happened, and the absent CLOCK line is the same refusal
to claim a duration nobody observed." So the evidence is kept and the duration is deliberately not
claimed. (An earlier statement in conversation that such a span "records nothing" was wrong.)

**Which means the active-marking question is a policy reversal, not a formatting change**, and it
must answer the measurement that produced the current policy rather than pass it by.
=--review-format-annotation= says "Always *inactive* timestamps, so nothing written from the queue
reaches =org-agenda=", and it says so because an active branch **existed and was removed**: it
branched on =:agent=, testing "is this a subagent" while claiming to test "is this a human", and on
2026-08-14 all 68 events of one session carried =agent_id= nil — so every span it produced was
published to the agenda as though the user had been at the keyboard. Its conclusion is the sentence
this proposal contradicts: *"there is no case in which a queue-derived span is the user's own
attention, and no branch to make."*

*The mechanism is not the obstacle.* =c084553c= established that an active timestamp inside
=:LOGBOOK:= does reach the agenda, and the docstring confirms that remains the mechanism — "reserved
for intervals a human logs themselves". So the edit is small; the argument is the expensive part.

*The distinction that keeps =01849bef= clear of this.* A **keystroke** is a human logging their own
interval, which the current design already sanctions — =4f8500e6= notes a human clocking in Emacs
writes a bare CLOCK line with no annotation at all. Only the **automatic** half asks the queue to
produce something the design says only a human may produce. So the manual half can ship without
reopening any of this; this occurrence decides the other half.

*What the September pass therefore has to establish*, and it is a higher bar than "is there a
pattern": evidence that distinguishes the human's attention **without inferring it from a field that
means something else**, which is exactly how the removed branch failed. =AFK= markers, an apply
timestamp inside the gap (=996fd2bd=) and the transcript are the candidates; =409a69ff= already
records why the first of those is fuzzier than it looks.
